title: The scent of rain
text: Almost everyone knows the smell of rain arriving on dry ground, and the phenomenon has a name: petrichor, {{1}} by Australian scientists in 1964. The smell is not the rain itself. Dry soil is coated with {{2}} — oils exuded by plants during droughts that settle on the earth like a lid. When the first drops land, they {{3}} tiny air bubbles that rise and burst, {{4}} the accumulated oils into a fine aerosol that the wind carries for kilometres. Humans are astonishingly {{5}} to it: we can detect the main compound, geosmin, at concentrations of five parts per trillion, and some researchers {{6}} that our ancestors needed to track water across dry country. The molecule's other claim to fame is {{7}}: geosmin is the earthy taste in beetroot and the off-taste in drinking water, famously hard to remove. Camels, it is said, can smell water fifty kilometres away; we can smell the promise of it from the next street. Either way, the scent {{8}} something older than language: after long drought, almost every culture on earth calls rain good news.

gaps.explanation: 'petrichor, named by scientists in 1964' — formally given the name; notarise = certify a document.
'coated with residues — oils exuded by plants' — the material left over; requisition = an official demand for supplies.
'drops capture tiny air bubbles' — catch them; capitulate = surrender.
'burst, flinging the oils into a fine aerosol' — hurling them out; foist takes 'on' (impose deceptively).
'humans are astonishingly attuned to it' — finely sensitive to it; attired = dressed.
'some researchers theorise that our ancestors needed to track water' — propose explanations; terrorise frightens, tolerate accepts, and testify is for courts.
'its other claim to fame is culinary' — to do with food and taste; culminate takes 'in'.
'the scent touches something older than language' — reaches it emotionally; topple = knock over.
